frus-1864p1:
The 1864 papers open with Great Britain, and Britain fills all of Part I. The correspondence runs through the war's hardest naval disputes. The Alexandra case opens the file. British-built ships for the Confederacy dominate the letters. Laird Brothers and their ironclad rams get a long section. The Rappahannock and the Pampero recur throughout.

Other papers handle men as well as ships. Britain protests enlistment of its seamen on the Kearsarge at Queenstown. Recruiting in Ireland draws sharp exchanges. The seizure of the steamer Chesapeake fills its own run. Adams in London presses Seward's case week by week. The volume shows neutrality strained to its limit. Every letter turns on keeping Britain out of the war.
frus-1865p1:
Part I of the 1865 papers pairs a presidential message with one great file. President Johnson opens the volume in grief. He marks Lincoln's death and the war's end. The correspondence that follows is all Great Britain. It runs to hundreds of documents. Adams and Seward carry the exchange.

The British file works through the war's residue. Neutrality duties fill Earl Russell's long letters. London holds to its declared course as ports change hands. Claims over ships and seizures await settlement. The tone shifts as the Confederacy collapses. What began as crisis management becomes accounting. This volume is the Anglo-American record of the war's last phase. It shows two governments stepping back from the brink.
frus-1866p1:
Part I of the 1866 papers joins a presidential message to seven files. Great Britain and its legation lead the correspondence. France and Mexico follow close behind. The French legation, Russia, and the Netherlands appear. China, Spain, and Austria complete the volume. Johnson's message reports peace restored across the Union. It also claims slavery extinguished by amendment.

Mexico gives the volume its tension. French papers debate the empire's collapse there. Reports say Maximilian may abdicate if terms fail. Paris promises to withdraw its troops in stages. Washington presses while France retreats. The British files handle the war's leftover claims. Together the papers show a republic turning outward again. Its first postwar quarrel is already under way.
frus-1867p1:
Part I of the 1867 papers pairs the presidential message with the European file. Great Britain takes the longest run. Adams reports talks with Lord Stanley on settling the Alabama claims. Fenian alarms in Ireland thread the letters. France follows, with its own legation papers. A special block covers the International Monetary Conference. It met at Paris in June 1867 to debate a common gold coin.

Russia, the Netherlands, and China come next. Spain, Austria, and Prussia have solid sections. Italy, Belgium, Denmark, Portugal, and Rome round out the part. The monetary papers argue over a five-franc gold unit. One delegate doubts any single coin will ever rule. The volume mixes old claims with new projects. Postwar America is testing its wider role.
frus-1868p1:
The 1868 papers open with the presidential message and a British problem. American citizens sit in British prisons as Fenian suspects. Warren, Nagle, and Costello name the leading cases. An attempt to blow up Clerkenwell prison sharpens the crisis. Seward presses the rights of naturalized citizens. Adams answers from London and tenders his resignation. The naturalization question runs beside the Alabama claims.

France and Russia take the next sections. China and Japan close Part I, Japan at length. The British file also looks toward settlement. One long letter weighs arbitration for the Alabama demands. A friendly government's judgment, it argues, would settle the principle best. The volume catches two disputes nearing resolution. Fenian prisoners and Confederate cruisers dominate its pages.
frus-1872p1:
Part I of the 1872 papers opens with proclamations and a broad country list. Mexico takes by far the longest run. Its papers report Porfirio Diaz in revolt. His November proclamation calls republican troops to rise. Russia and Salvador follow at a distance. The British sections break into special topics. One covers the boundary from the Lake of the Woods to the Rockies.

Fisheries near British North America get their own file. So does the slave trade on Africa's east coast. Another file asks how the flag flew on a seized schooner. Turkey's section adds a somber file. It prints consular letters on the persecution of Jews in Roumania. Grant's message notes peace at home and abroad. The volume blends routine posts with live disputes.
frus-1888p1:
Part I of the 1888 papers opens the Constitution's centennial year. Cleveland marks one hundred years of constitutional government. He warns that survival alone proves nothing. The files then run from Argentina toward Haiti. China overwhelms every other section. Its legation correspondence adds a second large block. Central America takes the next-largest run.

France and Germany both file at length. Haiti closes the part with a deep section. A mid-volume argument digs into Central American law. It asks whether Nicaragua's 1858 constituent assembly could alter boundaries. The decree, it argues, formed part of the constitution itself. Such legal archaeology fills these volumes. Part I ends mid-alphabet, at Haiti. The rest of the world waits for Part II.
frus-1894app1:
Appendix I to the 1894 papers gathers five special subjects. The Chinese-Japanese war leads the volume. Letters from Seoul open the file in April 1893. Heard and Allen report Korea sliding toward war. Fur seal enforcement follows at great length. Bluefields and the Mosquito Territory take the third block. The Mora claim against Spain fills the fourth.

Import duties close the main list. Colombia, Haiti, and Venezuela protest certain American duties. Samoa then returns in a long tail of papers. Pauncefote's 1891 communication to Blaine anchors one run. German embassy correspondence matches it in size. The appendix shows how special files outgrew the annual volume. War, seals, and islands each demanded their own record. It is a supplement with a war at its head.
frus-1895p1:
Part I of the 1895 papers runs from Argentina toward the alphabet's middle. Boundary awards open the volume. Cleveland decided the Misiones dispute between Argentina and Brazil. A separate heading prints his Brazil boundary decision. Britain's seizure of Trinidad island draws protest papers. China then takes the volume's bulk. Antiforeign riots fill its longest run.

Missionaries shelter on Russian territory in one file. American troops guard the legation in another. Austria-Hungary's papers turn on passports as proof of citizenship. Judges, the file asks, may disregard them or not. Two named citizenship cases anchor the debate. Belgium bans American cattle again. The part closes amid riot reports and claims. China's violence dominates the year's first half.
frus-1902app1:
Appendix I of 1902 prints an arbitration against Russia. Four American vessels claim seizure on the high seas. The whaling bark Cape Horn Pigeon leads the cases. A Russian vessel took her in the Sea of Okhotsk. She sat detained at Vladivostok through the season. The schooner James Hamilton Lewis was confiscated outright. The C. H. White met detention and confiscation too.

Russian cruisers took sealskins from the Kate and Anna. The Dutch counselor Asser heard the dispute. Claimant and defendant exchange memoranda, rejoinder, and surrejoinder. One paper fixes a seizure by chart and coordinates. The spot lay over eighty miles from Russian islands, it argues. The volume is a lawyer's duel over northern waters.
frus-1906p1:
Part I of the 1906 papers opens with disaster at home. San Francisco's earthquake and fire head the President's message. Circulars reorganize the consular service by statute. Shanghaiing is outlawed in another act. Secretary Root's tour of South America fills a file. Argentina marks a president's death and a vice-president's succession. Austria-Hungary fights over Hungarian emigrant transport.

China's mid-volume papers reckon opium revenue in taels. Native opium output is estimated by the picul. The duty converts between two kinds of taels. Imperial and customs treasuries split the take. Such arithmetic underlies Peking's finances. Belgium revisits the spirits trade in Africa. The part blends catastrophe, ceremony, and revenue. It runs from Argentina toward mid-alphabet.
frus-1907p1:
Part I of the 1907 papers begins with rules for citizens abroad. Expatriation and registration fill the circulars. Fraudulent naturalization reports draw their own heading. The Atlantic Fleet's cruise to the Pacific is announced. Argentina then takes the floor. A rejected shipment of deviled ham fills twenty documents. Argentine customs rules and railway concessions follow.

China's mid-volume demand concerns Mukden. That city now stands open to foreign trade. Goods that paid import duty, Washington argues, must move freely there. Treatment equal to other open ports is claimed. Austria debates universal suffrage in its section. A military service case names Peter Szatkowski. The part runs from Argentina into mid-alphabet. Pork, passports, and port rights fill its pages.
frus-1948v01p1:
Part 1 of Volume I for 1948 covers general policy and the United Nations. It opens with how the American mission was run and what role Washington saw for the world body. Headquarters loans and legal status fill the next sections.

Elections to UN organs, new members, and budget shares take long runs. The change in Czechoslovakia's delegation after the Prague coup appears. Human rights at the General Assembly and atomic control close the part. The papers show routine machinery and Cold War strain sharing the same agenda, often in the same week.
frus-1948v05p1:
Part 1 of Volume V for 1948 covers the Near East and the start of South Asia. The Palestine question heads the contents, and its full record fills the companion part. Oil growth and the Pentagon talks with Britain frame the region here.

Iran follows, with Soviet hostility and American political backing. Saudi aid and the Dhahran airfield lease take their own run. Kashmir and Hyderabad open the South Asia block, with long mediation papers. The volume catches new states being born amid war and partition. Smaller Gulf and Levant files fill out the Near East run.
frus-1949v07p1:
Part 1 of Volume VII for 1949 covers the Far East and Australasia, with Southeast Asia at its core. Indonesia dominates, as its fight against Dutch rule reached the Security Council and ended in recognition. Hundreds of papers track truce bids and talks.

Indochina's revolt against French return fills the next block. The Philippines appears in a short run on joint work with Washington. Study foundations in Australia and New Zealand close the part. Consular reports show empires ending by deal in one land and by war in another. Short accord sections close out the Australasia files.
frus-1951v03p1:
Part 1 of Volume III for 1951 covers European security and the German question. NATO's growth leads, from aid for Western Europe to the Ottawa and Rome council sessions. Greece and Turkey move toward joining in these pages.

A German share in Western defense takes the second half. The Paris talks on a European Defense Community fill long runs. Four-power feelers at the Palais Rose also appear. Three-power ministers met at Washington that fall. The papers show rearmament argued clause by clause, with France torn between fear and need. Council minutes let readers follow each vote.
frus-1951v04p1:
Europe's political and economic course fills Part 1 of Volume IV for 1951. Union drives lead, from the OEEC and the Payments Union to the Schuman Plan's final push. A coal crisis and surplus population plans sit beside them.

France takes the longest country run, with visits by Pleven and Auriol and aid for its arms program. Iceland's defense pact, Italy's treaty revision, and Spain's path toward Western defense follow. Trieste policy runs through the part. The papers show a continent knitting itself together with American money and urging. The part closes as the alliance debate hardens into signed plans.
frus-1951v06p1:
Asia and the Pacific fill Part 1 of Volume VI for 1951. Regional pacts lead, with defense deals for the Philippines and for Australia and New Zealand. Japan then takes the longest run, on its peace treaty and the linked security pact.

Indochina draws growing aid for French Union forces. Indonesia and Burma fill shorter country blocks. Korea's war runs beneath the whole part, named in the contents as a standing concern. The papers show a ring of pacts being built around a war that would not end, port by port and capital by capital.
frus-1951v07p1:
Part 1 of Volume VII for 1951 is the Korean War, told in dated blocks. The year opens with China branded an aggressor at the United Nations. The firing of General MacArthur follows in the spring sections, with the debate over the 38th parallel.

Truce talks begin in July, stall in August, and resume at Panmunjom in the fall. A demarcation line wins agreement, while prisoners block the rest. The so-called Black Book cables between Ridgway and the Joint Chiefs anchor the record. Readers see a war settle into talks without settling its cause.
frus-1952-54v01p1:
Part 1 of Volume I for 1952–1954 covers general economic and political matters. A short opening tracks the change of administrations in late 1952 and early 1953. Broad economic policy follows, from trade and investment to money questions.

Transport and communications policy take their own block. Aid under the Mutual Security Program closes the part, with hundreds of papers on how help was planned and justified. The record shows two presidents' teams working the same levers. Trade, aid, and growth were treated as parts of one contest with the Soviet bloc. The part's files end with the new team's first budget fights joined.
frus-1952-54v02p1:
Part 1 of Volume II for 1952–1954 is a single subject: national security policy. Objectives, threat studies, military posture, and the machinery for security fill the whole part. Policy Planning Staff and Council files anchor the record.

Readers can trace the shift from the Truman program to the Eisenhower New Look in the drafts. Papers weigh cost against reach and candor against morale at home and abroad. The part is dense by design. It prints the core texts where the long rivalry's ground rules were set, argued, and reset for a new team.
frus-1952-54v05p1:
Part 1 of Volume V for 1952–1954 covers Western European security through NATO's early growth. The Lisbon council session of February 1952 leads, with its London groundwork told meeting by meeting. Force goals and a German share drive the talks.

Acheson, Eden, Schuman, and Adenauer move through the minutes in turn. The part prints records, messages to the President, and tabled drafts. Readers see an alliance setting targets it strained to meet. The German question sits inside each agenda item, whether named or not, shaping what allies could promise each other. Trade curbs with the bloc fill the part's later economic files.
frus-1952-54v06p1:
Western Europe and Canada share Part 1 of Volume VI for 1952–1954. Union drives lead again, with aid for defense under the Mutual Security Program. Chiefs of mission met at London, Luxembourg, Vienna, and Copenhagen in these years.

Britain takes the closing block, from the Truman-Churchill talks of January 1952 to the Butler-Eden talks a year later. Money aid and Commonwealth counsel fill the cables. The papers show the senior partner short of cash and the junior partner paying more of the bills, a shift both sides felt and few named.
frus-1952-54v07p1:
Part 1 of Volume VII for 1952–1954 covers Germany and Austria, with the contract deals at the front. Talks led to the May 1952 signing at Bonn, printed here with the texts. A note war with Moscow on unity and votes follows.

Policy papers then weigh Bonn's place in Western defense and the 1953 federal vote. The Berlin Conference of early 1954 fills the last block, with groundwork, floor records, and post-mortems. The papers show a divided land argued over in set terms, while each half armed and settled into its camp. The part ends as the Saar and German questions move toward settlement.
frus-1952-54v09p1:
Part 1 of Volume IX for 1952–1954 covers the Near and Middle East at the regional level. Secretary Dulles's May 1953 tour with Harold Stassen opens the record. Plans for a regional defense system follow, laying the base for the Baghdad design.

Oil growth takes the next block, with tanker and concession fights. Arab-Israeli tension fills the largest run, from ties with each state to Eric Johnston's water missions. The papers show a new team testing a new map. Old British primacy fades through these files, replaced by American plans and local pushback.
frus-1952-54v11p1:
Africa fills Part 1 of Volume XI for 1952–1954, under the joint title Africa and South Asia. Regional policy leads, with reports from south of the Sahara and papers on French North Africa. Tangier's status and the Gold Coast follow.

Tunisia takes the longest run, on its clash with France at the United Nations. Morocco and Algeria, where revolt began in November 1954, come next. Ethiopia, Liberia, Libya, and South Africa fill the rest. The papers show a continent still ruled from Europe, with national claims rising in each file. The part's last files turn to the islands' place in Pacific defense.
frus-1952-54v12p1:
Part 1 of Volume XII for 1952–1954 is the regional record for East Asia and the Pacific. General policy fills the whole part, from ANZUS work and five-power staff talks to the Southeast Asia Collective Defense Treaty. Aid reviews run beside the pact work.

The papers show a web of deals being woven after the Korean War. Each ally's price and each frontier's risk appear in the drafts. Planners wrote of one region, but the files split by harbor and capital. The part is the blueprint room for the alliance system that followed.
frus-1952-54v14p1:
Part 1 of Volume XIV for 1952–1954 covers the China area by year. The 1952 block weighs Taiwan policy, aid to Nationalist forces, and trade curbs on the mainland. Jailed Americans in China recur through the files.

The 1953 block brings a new Seventh Fleet directive and a pledge that Taipei would consult before big attacks. Offshore island defense grows as a theme. Geneva talks on nationals and a draft defense pact close the part. The record shows a shield being drawn around one China while the other was shut out. The part closes with the armistice's terms still argued line by line.
frus-1952-54v15p1:
Part 1 of Volume XV for 1952–1954 is Korea, from stalemate to the edge of peace. The voluntary return of prisoners becomes the core fight at Panmunjom. A package deal is offered, then talks recess in the fall of 1952.

The Menon plan at the United Nations and its rejection by Peiping follow. A new team in Washington weighs wider war in NSC papers. Little Switch and the final POW deal close the part. Cables between Clark and Washington anchor the record. The war's last year was fought as much at the table as in the field.
frus-1955-57v23p1:
Japan fills Part 1 of Volume XXIII of the 1955–1957 set. Policy papers in the NSC 5516 line lead the record. Tokyo's renewed ties with Moscow and its wish for Okinawa's return fill long runs.

War criminals, textile imports, and Japan-Korea friction also appear. The Girard case closes the list of sore points. A mid-sample talk shows the Ryukyus held as not open to bargaining. The part shows a rich ally pressing for full standing, and a patron weighing bases against goodwill with each new file. Kishi's visit frames the part's close in the files.
frus-1958-60v07p1:
Western European integration and security, with Canada, fill Part 1 of Volume VII of the 1958–1960 set. The Common Market's growth and the birth of the OECD lead. Chiefs of mission met in Paris and London in 1958 on the change.

NATO takes the middle block, on council talks and joint plans. Canada closes the part, with the Seaway and Diefenbaker's 1960 visit. A mid-sample note catches France pulling at the alliance. The part shows two projects, market and alliance, growing side by side. Chiefs of mission spoke freely in the closed sessions here.
